newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian justice on trial in child sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Belgian justice on trial in child sex scandal.

text.p: Belgian justice went on trial on Tuesday as commentators reacted against a move by the lawyer defending chief child sex scandal suspect Marc Dutroux to get the investigating magistrate thrown off the case.

Lawyer Julien Pierre has formally asked for magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte to be removed on the grounds of bias because he did not pay for a dinner he was invited to by a support group for the parents of missing and murdered children.

"This manoeuvre is simply a new example of justice being taken hostage by the misuse of the legal means put at the disposal of the defence," Jean-Pierre Malmendier of the Marc et Corinne support group, said.
"Isn't it more important to establish the rights of the victims?" he asked Belgian media.

Malmendier accepted that Connerotte and public prosecutor Michel Bourlet had not payed for their spaghetti dinner on September 21, but he rejected claims by Pierre that they had contributed to a fund for the children.
Newspapers reported on Tuesday that there had been unprecedented public demonstrations in support of Connerotte and Bourlet -- an indication of the depth of feelings in the scandal.
Lawyer Pierre, who took the case after several others had turned it down, has received threatening telephone calls.

The unmasking of the child abduction, sexual abuse and murder ring allegedly led by convicted child rapist Dutroux has left Belgium in a state of shock and prompted hitherto unasked questions about the moral and political health of the country.
Four young girls have so far been found dead -- two at least starved to death -- and two others have been rescued alive.
Police have also unearthed the body of a former accomplice whom Dutroux admits killing, and are actively searching for at least seven other missing children.
The case has revealed a catalogue of bungling, incompetence and rivalry between different police forces and the judiciary, and prompted allegations of possible police complicity.
The arrest late on Monday of gendarme Gerard Vannesse on charges of drug trafficking and car theft -- the other side of the Dutroux dossier -- will have done nothing to dispel the fears.

Vannesse was the 13th person -- and the second policeman -- to be arrested and charged in the case. Seven people, including Dutroux, his second wife Michelle Martin and flamboyant businessman Jean-Michel Nihoul remain in detention.
Belgian newspapers reported that unemployed father-of-three Dutroux had millions of francs stashed in bank accounts around the country.
The Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court, will have to decide whether to uphold Pierre's complaint against Connerotte.
If it does so then Bourlet will almost certainly be forced to stand down as well, and the investigations severely hampered.

But even if the court rejects the move, the early tabling of the motion against Connerotte leaves open the possibility of a later appeal to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, which could prolong the case for years.
That is an eventuality that few Belgians would relish -- uncomfortable as they already are due to the glare of adverse international publicity created by the case.
